page.title: Creative agency vs production company decision guide
page.description: Compare capabilities, ownership, hidden dependencies and contract questions to choose the right partner for your event or content project.
page.h1: Creative agency versus production company: how to decide
page.definition: A creative agency is a strategic partner that develops brand concepts, messaging and design systems while a production company focuses on technical execution, crew management and live delivery of events or media. It also handles post‑production editing, asset management and distribution planning.
page.quick_answer: Start by mapping your project’s strategic scope to the partner that owns that capability, then verify who controls the run‑of‑show and backup stream.

sections.h2: What core capabilities separate a creative agency from a production company?

blocks.p: A creative agency owns strategy, brand voice and design systems while a production company owns crew, equipment and live‑stream operations.

ul: Visual identity and design system creation
Live event technical direction and crew staffing
Streaming platform configuration and backup stream management

sections.h2: Which ownership model fits your project timeline and budget?

blocks.p: If you need end‑to‑end brand development choose an agency; if you need a turnkey live event choose a production company.

ol: Define the primary deliverable: concept or live broadcast
Estimate the planning window: weeks for concept, days for technical rehearsal
Identify who approves creative assets versus who approves run‑of‑show
Match budget tiers: agency retainers versus production day rates
Select the partner that owns the critical path for your deadline

sections.h2: How do hidden dependencies affect delivery risk?

blocks.p: Hidden dependencies appear when creative assets must be formatted for a specific streaming platform or when rehearsal schedules clash with venue AV.

head: Dependency
Owner
rows: Creative asset formatting for platform specs

sections.h2: What questions should you ask before signing a contract?

blocks.p: Ask who owns the run‑of‑show, who provides the backup stream, and how revisions are scoped.

ul: Which party writes and approves the run‑of‑show document?
Who supplies and tests the redundant streaming path?
How many revision rounds are included for creative assets?
What are the escalation steps if a technical failure occurs live?
Who holds the final sign‑off on post‑event deliverables?

sections.h2: When does a hybrid approach make sense?

blocks.p: A hybrid model works when you need strategic concept work from an agency and reliable live execution from a production company.

Engage the agency early to lock brand narrative and design system, then hand off finalized assets to the production company for platform build, rehearsal management and live delivery. This split keeps creative iteration separate from technical risk and lets each specialist own its quality gate.

faq.q: Can one firm handle both strategy and live production?
faq.a: Some shops offer both but usually split teams; verify that the same people will not be stretched across creative reviews and live‑stream operations on the same day.

faq.q: How do I evaluate a production company’s backup stream capability?
faq.a: Request a documented redundancy plan, ask for a recent test recording of the failover path, and confirm they monitor both streams simultaneously during the event.

faq.q: What contract clauses protect against scope creep?
faq.a: Include a defined deliverable list, a revision limit with change‑order process, and a clear acceptance criteria for each milestone before payment release.

faq.q: Does West Peek Productions offer both creative and production services?
faq.a: West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations; it does not sell event software.
